meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life is not fair; get used to it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bill Gates. Wikiquote says the list of blunt life rules is based on one from the American writer Charles J. Sykes.

answer.label: Not Bill Gates — actually Charles J. Sykes
answer.authorDates: Born 1954 · American author and political commentator
answer.sourceLine: The line travels as one of a set of blunt life rules said to come from a Bill Gates speech to high-school students. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and says the list is actually based on one from Charles J. Sykes. Which of Sykes’s books or columns first carried it, we could not establish.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bill Gates, in a high-school speech

source.excerpt: Life is not fair. Get used to it... Be nice to nerds. Chances are you'll end up working for one.
trail: Wikiquote’s Bill Gates page ↗ lists this line under Misattributed, and says that although the list is widely attributed to Gates on the internet, it “is actually based on one from Charles J. Sykes”.
Wikiquote’s note points to a Snopes fact-check for the fuller story. That page is unreachable from our network, so we have not read it and do not repeat its findings here.

Sykes is a real and identifiable writer — his bibliography ↗ includes Dumbing Down Our Kids (1995) and 50 Rules Kids Won’t Learn in School (2007) — but we could not confirm which work first published this list, so no specific work is claimed here.
source.excerptNote: The wording above is the entry exactly as it stands in Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗, which quotes two of the rules from the circulating list.
source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted, because we could not tie this wording to a specific publication. If the list is Charles J. Sykes’s, as Wikiquote says, it would be modern and in copyright; the version that circulates under Gates’s name has no identified publisher at all.

author.name: Charles J. Sykes
author.heading: About Charles J. Sykes
author.metaLine: Born 1954 · American author, radio host and political commentator
author.bio: Charles Jay Sykes (born 11 November 1954 in Seattle) is an American author and political commentator. He hosted a conservative talk show on Milwaukee’s WTMJ from 1993 to 2016 and later served as editor-in-chief of The Bulwark. His books on American schooling include Dumbing Down Our Kids (1995) and 50 Rules Kids Won’t Learn in School (2007).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: It is one of the most forwarded pieces of advice on the internet, and it arrives with a famous name welded to the front of it. The name is wrong.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed ↗, noting that although it is widely attributed to Gates on the internet, the list is not his.

misattribution.truthLine: Wikiquote credits the list to the writer Charles J. Sykes rather than to Bill Gates — see the entry ↗. Which of Sykes’s works first published it we could not establish, and none is claimed here.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The rules spread because the attribution flattered them. Advice about the unfairness of life lands differently when it seems to come from the richest man in the world addressing teenagers — it reads as hard-won, and slightly cruel, and therefore true.
Strip the name away and it is a working writer’s argument about American schooling, which is what Wikiquote says it always was.
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s entry is careful in a way the internet version is not: it says the list is “based on” one from Charles J. Sykes, and it does not name a book. We have kept to that limit here rather than filling the gap with the book title that usually accompanies the claim.
context.pull: The advice was not improved by the name attached to it.
